title: what the string is for
hookLine: beads on a rearview mirror: counting, not magic

lines: ON A MIRROR. IN A PURSE.
cards: A loop of beads swinging from a rearview mirror. Tangled in a grandmother's purse with the car keys and the cough drops. Laid in someone's hands at a funeral.
Some people wear one like a necklace; some call it a lucky charm. People can't even agree how many beads are on it. The string is for something much plainer than luck.

teach.b: Rosary comes from the Latin rosarium, a rose garden: a garland of prayers, like a crown of roses. Here's the layout.
A cross, a short tail of beads, then the loop: five sets of ten small beads, called decades, each set apart by a single bead. On the single bead, the Our Father. On each of the ten, a Hail Mary.
After each ten, a short line of praise, the Glory Be. One decade on its own takes about five minutes, and plenty of people start there.
That's where the arguments about the count come from: fifty-nine beads on the whole string, fifty-three Hail Marys. Counting prayers is ancient.
Stories from the early desert monks tell of one who kept track of his daily prayers with pebbles in his lap.

Later, monks prayed all one hundred and fifty psalms, and tradition says people who couldn't read prayed one hundred and fifty short prayers instead. The rosary grew out of that, and was called the poor man's psalter.

While the fingers and lips are busy with the words, the mind is free to think through scenes from the lives of Jesus and Mary, called the mysteries. That's the real prayer. The beads just keep the hands busy.

how: Catholics pray the rosary alone or together, some every day, saying an Our Father, ten Hail Marys and a Glory Be for each decade while thinking about a scene from the life of Jesus and Mary.

games.q: what's on the string — tap the pairs.
p: scenes from the lives of Jesus and Mary

s: the rosary is a good-luck charm
the beads are a counting tool. the prayer is in the words and the mysteries.
a rosary has fifty-nine beads, but you say fifty-three Hail Marys
fifty in the loop and three on the tail are Hail Marys; the other beads carry other prayers.
desert monks counted prayers with pebbles
one story tells of a monk keeping count with pebbles in his lap.

games.q: you're a medieval farmer. the monks pray all 150 psalms, but you can't read and have no book. what do you do?
o: pay a monk to pray for you.
pray 150 short prayers, counted on a string.
games.why: that's how tradition says the rosary grew. people called it the poor man's psalter.

games.q: put one decade back in order.

practice: Three breaths with the bell. Rest one hand in your lap. On each breath out, touch your thumb to the next finger: one, two, three.
Don't count out loud. Let the fingers keep track, so the mind doesn't have to.

wordCard.voice: The rosary. A garland of prayers on a string that keeps count, so the mind can rest on the life of Jesus. Fourth word.

orig.note: Latin: a rose garden, a garland of roses. the rosary as a crown of prayers.

carryVoice: Your line: hands busy, heart free. The beads hold the count, so the mind can go somewhere better. That's day four.
